extracted.intended_audience: biosimilar applicants, reference product sponsors, and patent litigators in the pharmaceutical/biotech industry
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on the BPCIA 'patent dance' process for exchanging aBLA information, identifying patents for potential litigation, and the timing and consequences of participating or opting out. Useful for counsel advising biosimilar applicants or reference product sponsors on statutory steps, rights, and risks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patent Dance framework (exchange of aBLA confidential information)
rubrics_metrics.description: The BPCIA provides a framework that includes certain steps and a schedule during which the applicant and reference product sponsor exchange confidential information disclosed in the aBLA.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: During the patent dance, the applicant and sponsor identify the patents that could be litigated in the future. The process is procedural and involves timed exchanges of application and manufacturing information (the aBLA) between the parties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Two-phase patent-identification and assertion structure
rubrics_metrics.description: During the patent dance the applicant and sponsor identify patents that could be litigated in two potential phases: (1) in the first phase the sponsor can allege infringement of a subset of the patents identified during the patent dance; (2) the second phase begins after the sponsor receives the Notice of Commercial Marketing from the applicant, when the sponsor can assert any remaining patents not asserted in the first phase.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The statutory scheme allocates which patents may be asserted at which stage—planning for which patents to identify and which to assert is a key strategic element of complying with the BPCIA timeline and preserving rights.

rubrics_metrics.name: Duration/timeline if fully executed
rubrics_metrics.description: If both the applicant and the sponsor engage in all of the steps set forth in the BPCIA and take the maximum allotted time, the patent dance can take up to 250 days (approximately eight months) to complete.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Parties should account for up to ~250 days when planning regulatory and litigation strategy if they follow every step and use maximum time allotments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patent dance is not mandatory (Amgen v. Sandoz)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Supreme Court held that the patent dance is not mandatory. Although the BPCIA requires that an applicant 'must' provide its application and manufacturing information, the statute also 'provides a remedy for an applicant’s failure to turn over its application and manufacturing information.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Counsel should be aware that the applicant may opt not to engage in the dance; the statutory text and Supreme Court precedent mean participation is optional and has legal consequences (see Amgen v. Sandoz, Nos. 15-1039, 15-1195).

rubrics_metrics.name: Consequences of opting out of the patent dance
rubrics_metrics.description: If the applicant eschews the dance, the decision of when and which patents to litigate shifts to the sponsor, who retains the right to immediately seek 'a declaration of infringement, validity, or enforceability of any patent that claims the biological product or a use of the biological product.' (42 U.S.C. § 262(l)(9)(C)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Opting out also foregoes certain possible restrictions on damages recovery (see 35 U.S.C. § 271(e)(6)). In contrast, engaging in the dance preserves certain procedural rights for the applicant (see next entry). Parties should weigh litigation timing, remedies, and damages exposure when deciding whether to participate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect of participating: preservation of declaratory judgment rights
rubrics_metrics.description: If the applicant engages in the dance, the applicant preserves the right to file a declaratory judgment action to challenge the validity of the identified patents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Participation can preserve the applicant’s ability to proactively challenge patents identified during the exchange; this is a strategic consideration when balancing the benefits of information exchange against risks of giving the sponsor litigation leverage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Notice of Commercial Marketing requirement and timing
rubrics_metrics.description: The BPCIA requires that a biosimilar applicant 'shall provide notice to the reference product sponsor not later than 180 days before the date of the first commercial marketing of the biological product licensed under subsection (k).' (42 U.S.C. § 262(l)(8)(A)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Per the Supreme Court (Sandoz Slip Op. at 16), the applicant may provide this notice either before or after receiving FDA approval; the applicant need not wait until after FDA approval/licensure to provide notice of intent to commercially market the biosimilar. Counsel should calendar the 180-day notification requirement relative to anticipated launch timing.
